common_name: R.L. Wheeler Camellia (Giant Rose-Pink Semi-Double to Peony-Form Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; R.L. Wheeler is prized for producing some of the largest flowers in the genus on a vigorous, upright plant.

directions: R.L. Wheeler is a long-standing exhibition favorite grown for its enormous, 5-6-inch semi-double to loose peony-form flowers in a clear, glowing rose-pink, produced abundantly through the midseason bloom window on a fast-growing, upright, well-branched shrub. Its large-flower genetics make it a common parent in camellia breeding programs, and its vigorous habit means it fills space in the landscape quickly compared to slower japonica cultivars. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to filtered light, and mulch well to keep roots cool and evenly moist. Prune lightly to shape immediately after flowering, since next season's buds set on the current year's growth.

common_name: Drama Girl Camellia (Enormous Waved Rose-Pink Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Drama Girl produces some of the largest flowers of any camellia cultivar and benefits from wind-sheltered placement to protect the huge blooms.

directions: Drama Girl lives up to its name with semi-double flowers that can reach 7 inches across, their wavy, crepe-textured rose-pink petals arranged in a loose, informal form that ages to a deeper pink at the margins. The plant itself is a strong, upright grower with large, leathery dark-green leaves proportioned to match its outsized blooms, flowering in mid to late season. Because the flowers are so heavy and broad, sheltering the shrub from strong wind and hot afternoon sun helps prevent petal damage and extends bloom life. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, water deeply during dry spells, and prune only right after bloom to preserve next year's flower buds.

common_name: Anacostia Camellia (Red and White Variegated Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Anacostia was introduced from the U.S. National Arboretum and is valued for its bold red-and-white marbled flowers.

directions: Anacostia bears medium-to-large semi-double to loose peony-form flowers in a bold red splashed and marbled irregularly with white, so no two blooms are quite alike, on a compact, well-behaved shrub with the dense, glossy foliage typical of Camellia japonica. It flowers over a long midseason stretch and holds its color well even in cooler weather. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to filtered light, keeping the root zone mulched and evenly moist through summer establishment. Prune only immediately after flowering to maintain shape, since flower buds for the following year form on new growth soon after bloom.

common_name: Bokuhan Camellia (Miniature Red Anemone-Form Higo Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Bokuhan is a classic Japanese heirloom prized for its tiny, tidy anemone-form flowers on a compact, slow-growing plant well suited to small gardens or containers.

directions: Bokuhan is a diminutive, centuries-old Japanese cultivar producing small, 2-inch, deep red single-to-anemone-form flowers with a tight cluster of tiny white petaloids at the center, giving each bloom a striking pinwheel-like contrast. The plant grows slowly into a dense, twiggy, small-leaved shrub that stays far more compact than most japonica cultivars, making it a natural choice for bonsai training, container culture, or foreground plantings. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and protect from harsh afternoon sun, which can bleach the deep red color. Prune lightly right after bloom to maintain its naturally dense, twiggy form.

common_name: Grace Albritton Camellia (Miniature Pale Pink Anemone-Form Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Grace Albritton is a miniature-flowered cultivar suited to small-space gardens, containers, or foreground plantings.

directions: Grace Albritton produces an abundance of small, formal-to-anemone-form flowers in a soft blush pink fading to near-white toward the petal edges, opening over a long midseason period on a compact, densely branched shrub with small, neat foliage. Its miniature flower size and restrained habit make it useful for smaller landscapes, mixed borders, or container specimens where the larger-flowered exhibition cultivars would be out of scale. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, keeping the root zone consistently moist and mulched. Prune lightly after flowering to keep its naturally tidy, rounded form.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Narumigata is one of the oldest and most widely grown sasanqua cultivars, valued for its large single flowers and late-fall bloom.

directions: Narumigata bears large, 3-inch single flowers in white delicately blushed with pink along the petal edges, opening around a prominent boss of golden stamens in a heavy fall flush and carrying a light, sweet fragrance uncommon among camellias. The upright, well-branched shrub tolerates more direct sun than most japonica types, and stronger light generally produces heavier bloom. Its vigorous, adaptable habit works well as a background shrub, informal screen, or espalier subject. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, and prune lightly to shape right after the fall bloom period ends.
